az_corndog_wall_the.blurb: A compact wall of roughly 30 feet in the Granite Dells outside Prescott, tucked into the Oasis section along the north edge of the Stairway Loop trail. Seventeen routes, mostly bolted sport lines with a few trad and top-rope options, stretch from easy fifth-class up into the 5.11s, with the bulk of them between 5.9 and 5.10. The granite is coarse and still cleaning up, and many lines have seen few ascents. The wall picks up sun from late morning into the evening in the busy season, so it suits a quick, short-approach session more than a long day.

az_wash_boulders.blurb: A small cluster of boulders in the Oak Flat bouldering zone of Queen Creek Canyon, east of Phoenix near Superior. Seventeen problems sit on a handful of free-standing blocks perched on rocky shelves, so a spare pad folded under your main one helps level the landings. The grades run low: most are VB to V1, with only a few reaching V2 through V4, which makes it a friendly place to warm up or bring newer boulderers. The volcanic welded tuff is abrasive, with plenty of small, unusual holds. Reach it by walking past the entrance boulders, then dropping into a small wash and climbing back up to the platform.

az_4_the_double_clutching_wall.blurb: A tall tan wall of columnar basalt just around the corner from the Right Wall in the Waterfall amphitheater, Oak Creek Canyon, between Sedona and Flagstaff. All 17 routes are trad, built on long splitter cracks, and the spread starts at 5.11 and climbs through the 5.12s into the low 5.13s, so this is a wall for strong leaders. It faces south and collects the most sun at the Waterfall, making it the pick for cool, calm days. Scrub oak above the climbs gives it more cover than neighboring walls. Allow a longer canyon walk to reach the amphitheater first, then a couple of minutes along the base.

az_swim_fin.blurb: A granite fin on the ridge below Windy Point on the Catalina Highway, Mount Lemmon, above Tucson. Its sixteen routes are mostly bolted, with a few trad lines, and run from easy 5.6 through 5.12; the largest group sits around 5.10, with a good number of moderates in the 5.7 to 5.9 range. Climbs line both faces of the rock, and one side usually holds shade depending on the hour and season. Many moderates in one spot make it popular, so expect to wait your turn on busy days. The walk in is short and begins right across the road from the overlook lot.
az_swim_fin.parking_note: Use the Windy Point overlook lot on the Catalina Highway, with restrooms. The trail starts by crossing the road to the guardrail.

az_monster_roof.blurb: A long, low band of limestone in Priest Draw, a shallow canyon south of Flagstaff, past Anorexic Roof. The middle is undercut into a steep roof while both ends stay near vertical, giving a mix of powerful pocket problems and gentler wall lines. Sixteen problems range from V1 up to V7, with most falling between V1 and V5 and a few harder test pieces at the top end. It is a boulder-only spot with one of the longer walks in the draw, and the back of the cave is littered with rodent droppings, so watch where you put pads and hands.
az_monster_roof.approach: Follow the main trail up Priest Draw for about 15 minutes. Continue beyond Anorexic Roof; this roof comes up next on your right.

az_south_park.blurb: A remote, quiet sport crag high on Mount Lemmon near the top end of the Catalina Highway, in the Upper Highway sector above Tucson. All 16 routes are bolted and the grades lean hard: a lone 5.8 and a 5.9 lead into a block of 5.10s, with the biggest group in the 5.11s and two 5.12s at the top end. Expect steep, blocky climbing with plenty of holds to pull on. The crag receives sun in the morning through midday, then falls into shade, which helps on warmer days. It sits well off the road and the walk in takes real effort, so it tends to be empty.
